sections.title: What changes at 3 to 4 years

blocks.title: Not from your PDFs
blocks.text: No guide of yours covers this, so this page was written for the site, as of October 2026. Tools and versions change quickly: check the official documentation before relying on details.

blocks: A fresher is asked **what** something is. At 3 to 4 years you are asked **why you chose it, what went wrong, and what you would change**. Knowing Spring is assumed; owning a service in production is what is being tested.

rows: Resizing cost, treeification, why you presize, and when you chose ConcurrentHashMap in a real service
Self-invocation, propagation, isolation anomalies you met, and keeping transactions away from remote calls
Partition key choice, duplicates, retries, a dead-letter topic, and how you handled consumer lag
The architecture, your part, the hardest bug, numbers, and what you would redesign
blocks.caption: The same topic, asked at two levels.

blocks.title: Common rounds
blocks.code:
flowchart LR
  A[Recruiter screen] --> B[Coding: DSA, medium level]
  B --> C[Java and Spring depth]
  C --> D[Low-level design or machine coding]
  D --> E[High-level design]
  E --> F[Project deep dive]
  F --> G[Manager and behavioural]
blocks.caption: Companies differ: service companies often skip design rounds, and product companies weigh coding and design more.

rows: Pattern recognition, clean Java, tests aloud

sections.title: How to use this site at your level

rows: Skim the basics; test yourself with the practice questions
Study properly, and map it to your projects
Indexes, plans, isolation, cache failure modes first
Failure handling and delivery guarantees first
Practise on paper, with a timer
Be able to deploy and defend an architecture
Enough to own a feature end to end
Only if your target company tests it
blocks.caption: My suggested emphasis, not a rule: adjust it to your target companies.

blocks.title: Skip by testing, not by assuming
blocks.text: Answer a part's practice questions before reading it. If you get them right, tick it off and move on.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Expect why, trade-offs and failures, not definitions.
- Tie every concept to something you built.
- Numbers you measured beat adjectives.
- Do DSA in parallel: 2 problems a day beats a final cram.

items.question: Why is "I used Redis for caching" a weak answer?
items.answer: It states a tool, not a decision. Say what was slow, what you cached, how you invalidated it, how you handled stampedes, and the measured result.

items.question: Which rounds are usually new compared with a fresher's interview?
items.answer: Low-level and high-level design, the project deep dive, and behavioural questions about ownership.
